A101.text:
El precio del petróleo Brent para contratos a enero del 2027 cayó este martes por debajo de los US$90 por barril, su valor más bajo desde agosto. Sucede ante las expectativas de un acuerdo entre Estados Unidos e Irán para poner fin a la guerra en Medio Oriente. La baja profundizó el retroceso de las últimas jornadas, aunque las negociaciones todavía tienen diferencias por resolver y los analistas advierten que una nueva escalada militar podría revertirlo.
El crudo del mar del Norte, referencia internacional y para el petróleo argentino, llegó a operar a US$89,66 durante la mañana, antes de recuperarse a poco más de US$90. En Estados Unidos, el West Texas Intermediate (WTI) para entrega en diciembre bajaba 2,82%, hasta US$84,40, de acuerdo con EFE.
El movimiento se produjo después de que el presidente Donald Trump afirmara que la guerra con Irán está “prácticamente terminada en el plano militar”. Lo dijo tras reunirse el lunes en Washington con el primer ministro y canciller de Catar, Mohamed bin Abdulrahman al Thani, cuyo país actúa como mediador en las conversaciones con Teherán.
Aunque aseguró que Estados Unidos sigue preparado para volver a atacar, Trump consideró “bastante improbable” una reanudación de las operaciones militares. Desde Catar confirmaron que hubo avances en las negociaciones.
Irán, por su parte, reclamó que Washington acepte sus condiciones para reabrir el estrecho de Ormuz, bloqueado desde el comienzo del conflicto a fines de febrero. Entre sus exigencias figuran el fin de las hostilidades en todos los frentes, la liberación de activos congelados, el levantamiento de las sanciones petroleras y el cese del bloqueo estadounidense sobre sus puertos.
Según Teherán, si Estados Unidos acepta esos términos, el paso marítimo podría reabrirse en dos días. El canciller iraní, Abás Araqchi, sostuvo que la salida debe llegar por la diplomacia y que el conflicto no se resolverá mediante acciones militares o nuevas sanciones.
Una baja de precios que todavía no despeja los riesgos
El cambio de expectativas ya había llevado al Brent desde casi US$118 a fines de octubre hasta alrededor de US$90 este martes. En un informe, Rystad Energy vinculó la corrección del crudo con el triunfo demócrata en las elecciones legislativas estadounidenses y el mayor costo político que tendría para Trump profundizar la guerra.
Pero la consultora advirtió que los precios se movieron más rápido que las condiciones del abastecimiento. Su estimación ubica las exportaciones de crudo del Golfo alrededor de un 20% por debajo de los niveles anteriores al conflicto. Además, señaló que persisten diferencias sustanciales sobre las sanciones, el programa nuclear iraní y las reglas para el tránsito comercial por Ormuz.
“El mercado está tratando la victoria demócrata como si hubiera resuelto la situación con Irán. No lo ha hecho”, afirmó Claudio Galimberti, economista jefe de Rystad. Según su análisis, lo que cambió es el costo político de una escalada, mientras siguen pendientes los problemas que originaron la tensión.
La firma mantiene su escenario de riesgo elevado de nuevas acciones militares en el corto plazo, seguido de un entendimiento limitado y una recuperación gradual de los flujos del Golfo durante 2027. También advierte que, antes de que asuma el nuevo Congreso el 3 de enero, Washington podría recurrir a la presión militar para intentar mejorar su posición negociadora.
La incertidumbre alcanza, además, a los combustibles. Rystad señaló que los nuevos ataques ucranianos contra refinerías rusas mantienen la presión sobre la producción de ese país y prolongan la estrechez del mercado mundial de gasoil, incluso mientras baja la cotización del crudo.

A107.text:
Gibran, the son of former president Joko Widodo, has come under intense scrutiny following rulings last month by the Constitutional Court and the Supreme Court saying that his education documents did not meet election requirements.
The controversy has unfolded amid a widening rift between Widodo, also known as Jokowi, and the current President Prabowo Subianto, fuelling speculation over Gibran's political future.
Gibran stated his intention to resign during a meeting with Prabowo on Tuesday.
Over 100 lawmakers from several parties in parliament have signed a petition stating that Gibran is not eligible for office because the court rulings mean he "no longer meets the requirements as VP candidate," said Muhammad Kholid, one of the lawmakers signing the petition.
The petition will be submitted to the House speaker, Kholid told Reuters, adding that the formal declaration of the lawmakers' position on the issue would lead into the impeachment process.
The Supreme Court said in a ruling published on its website late on Tuesday that it was instructing the education ministry to withdraw Gibran's education equivalence certificate, which the court has annulled.
Gibran, who studied abroad, used the certificate to comply with education requirements and run in the 2024 election, which he won alongside Prabowo.
Indonesian election law requires vice-presidential candidates to have completed senior high school or an equivalent level of education, but the court found that the certificate was issued based on evidence that did not actually prove Jokowi's eldest son had graduated.
"No evidence was found to show Gibran had a foreign diploma or certificate that could serve as the basis for equivalency with a senior high school or equivalent qualification," the court said in the ruling.
The Supreme Court also took into account the Constitutional Court's ruling, which said Gibran's education documents did not meet election requirements.
Sana Jaffrey, a researcher at Australian National University, said it would be difficult to imagine that lawmakers will move against Gibran without Prabowo's awareness or approval.
"Prabowo's silence suggests that he wants Gibran’s removal without bearing the potential political cost of openly engineering it, particularly a possible backlash from Jokowi supporters whose backing helped secure his victory," she said.
She said the crisis shows how the political fortunes of a small number of elites take precedence over the country’s need for effective and stable governance.
"Prolonged uncertainty at the highest levels of power will only deepen anxieties at home and abroad about where the country is headed," she said.
(Reporting by Ananda Teresia; Editing by David Stanway)

A11.text:
Chinese university buys Nvidia AI H200 chips despite US ban, records show
A Chinese defence-linked university bought two H200 chips last month, as scrutiny grows over Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged spy for Beijing.
A Chinese university with ties to the army bought Nvidia’s powerful H200 AI chips last month despite being on a US export blacklist.
Northwestern Polytechnical University, a member of China’s “Seven Sons of National Defense” group of elite defence-focused universities, bought two H200 chips last month for 874,700 yuan ($123,000), according to an October 21 procurement record on its website, the Reuters news agency reports.
The chips were bought for its management school from Shaanxi Bosuan Network Technology rather than directly from Nvidia, the record showed.
The Reuters investigation comes as Nvidia and its CEO Jensen Huang face mounting scrutiny in Washington, DC, over his lobbying for looser restrictions on sales of AI chips to China, following reports alleging he was targeted by a Chinese spying operation.
The H200 is among Nvidia’s most capable chips for training and running advanced AI systems and is subject to US export licence approvals, which are normally denied for blacklisted institutions such as Northwestern Polytechnical.
Northwestern Polytechnical also bought access this year to H200 chips and other powerful Nvidia AI processors through five contracts for rented computing capacity from Chinese companies, procurement records show.
Nvidia CEO Huang has argued that continued US sales to China would preserve US technological leadership and keep Chinese customers reliant on its technology.
However, some US lawmakers say access to Nvidia’s most powerful AI chips can speed China’s development of AI systems for weapons design, intelligence analysis and military modernisation.
US blacklist
Based in the northwestern city of Xi’an, Northwestern Polytechnical conducts research related to military aircraft, missiles and satellites.
Washington’s Department of Commerce added the university to its trade blacklist, known as the Entity List, in 2001 over the institute’s alleged involvement in missile-proliferation activities, and its military research. Washington tightened the restrictions in 2019, making licences for exporting controlled US technology to the university subject to a policy of denial in most circumstances.
Northwestern Polytechnical’s purchases show how Chinese institutions with military ties continue to obtain US AI computing power through domestic suppliers, either by buying chips outright or renting access to servers containing them.
A Reuters review of 26 Chinese procurement and corporate records from this year found universities and research institutions buying US-restricted Nvidia chips or renting access to Nvidia-powered computing services that use such chips through domestic suppliers.
Several had close links to China’s defence industry or military research.
US President Donald Trump’s administration began allowing some H200 exports to China on a case-by-case basis in January. But that policy did not lift the separate restrictions applying to Entity List organisations such as Northwestern Polytechnical.
Both Democrats and Republicans in the US Congress have urged stronger controls on China’s access to advanced AI chips, such as chip-tracking requirements, and greater congressional oversight of exports.
The Huang affair
This comes at a time of increased pressure on Nvidia’s Huang. Republican US Senator Kevin Cramer from the Senate Banking Committee called on Huang to step down as CEO after his intimate relationship with Alice Huang, accused of working for Chinese intelligence, plunged the company into crisis.
“The potential for extortion is so tremendous that something as sensitive as Nvidia chips, I just think he’s got to go,” Cramer told Politico late on Tuesday.

A132.text:
Hopes were high that the 31st Conference of the Parties (COP31) would build on the momentum of last year’s climate talks, which sought to triple the money developed nations contribute every year so the countries that contributed least to human-induced climate change could adapt and shield communities from a warming world.
However, after Brazil’s André Aranha Corrêa do Lago, who served as COP30 president, handed the gavel to Turkish Minister of Environment, Urbanisation and Climate Change, Murat Kurum, the current president, on Monday, 9 November, during the opening plenary parties failed to agree to put triple adaptation finance on the main agenda.
This is despite the fact that developed nations, particularly the European Union (EU) group, committed to putting triple finance on the agenda this year at the end of COP30 to iron out the details on how the increased funding would be reached.
At COP30, UN Framework Convention on Climate Change parties agreed to increase the amount of money earmarked for adaptation to between $85-billion and $120-billion annually by 2035.
However, South Africa and many developing countries in the Global South are pushing hard for guaranteed, trackable funding to help vulnerable nations build climate-resilient infrastructure, protect water sources and handle droughts before disasters strike.
As the deadlock was quietly developing behind closed doors in negotiation rooms, the Climate Action Network (CAN) held a press briefing about the stalemate.
“We’re coming into this COP while the world is burning. We have seen climate impacts throughout the year across the world getting more frequent and more devastating. We bear witness to this, and many of us have actually lived through this climate crisis and its impact,” said Climate Action Network Executive Director Tasneem Essop.
“However, we are already coming into this COP recognising that those who have obligations to deliver, the developed world, have already signalled that they will not be coming to this COP with any additional finance commitments,” she said.
Climate Action Network is an observer organisation in the COP and therefore knows what is happening in the negotiations that are closed to the public.
Speaking to Daily Maverick on the sidelines of events on Monday night, Sara Shaw, Director of Campaigns and Networks at climate advocacy organisation 350.org, said that while developing nations pushed and succeeded in getting broader climate finance on the agenda, the proposal to triple adaptation finance did not secure its own specific track on the agenda, creating procedural confusion and leaving it without a dedicated home.
“On the tripling of climate finance adaptation, I think it seemed like it was definitely out of the picture, and then it got a bit more confused this morning. It doesn’t have its own place on the agenda. Countries no doubt will bring it up in different parts of the agenda, but it hasn’t really got its own home. And so that is quite a problem because that was something that was a real commitment from developed countries last year. They kind of almost used it last year in order to get some agreement, but there’s so little precision about it. It’s such a vague commitment at the moment that I think countries were really, really keen that there was a time frame put on it,” Shaw said.
But that does not mean South Africa has abandoned its mission. The Department of Forestry, Fisheries and the Environment confirmed to Daily Maverick that the haggling, which SA’s lead negotiator Maesela Kekana was handling on behalf of the country, went well into the night and continued this morning as the African group and other interested parties fought to get on the agenda to ensure that the issue would be well aired throughout the negotiations, and would hopefully result in firm commitments by the end of the two-week conference.

A144.text:
Wegen Irankrieg Die Golfstaaten gründen militärischen Kommandoposten mit Sitz in Kuwait
Der Irankrieg sorgt für Wiederannäherungen auf der Arabischen Halbinsel: Die untereinander zerstrittenen sechs Staaten des Golfkooperationsrats (GCC) forcieren ihre militärische Zusammenarbeit.
Saudi-Arabien, die Vereinigten Arabischen Emirate, Katar und die anderen GCC-Länder einigten sich dafür auf die Gründung eines gemeinsamen Kommandopostens. Dieser soll in Kuwait entstehen, das dem Rat ebenso angehört wie Bahrain und Oman. Auch die »erforderlichen Truppen« sollen dafür bereitgestellt werden, hieß es nach einer Sitzung der GCC-Verteidigungsminister in Bahrains Hauptstadt Manama. Details oder Zahlen zur Truppenstärke wurden nicht genannt.
Die Sicherheit der Golfstaaten mit Blick auf die »brutale iranische Aggression« sei eine gemeinsame Aufgabe, sagte GCC-Generalsekretär Dschasim al-Budaiwi bei dem Treffen in Manama. Eine militärische Zusammenarbeit steigere die Fähigkeiten, Staatsgebiete, Vermögenswerte und Sicherheit der Bevölkerung in den Golfländern zu schützen.
Der Golfkooperationsrat wurde 1981 gegründet, nur zwei Jahre nach der iranischen Revolution 1979 und in der frühen Phase des Ersten Golfkriegs zwischen dem Irak und Iran. Schon zu Beginn standen Fragen zur gemeinsamen Sicherheit im Fokus. Wenige Jahre später wurden die »Halbinsel-Schutzkräfte» gegründet, die zeitweise 40.000 Soldaten umfassten und die 2011 bei der Niederschlagung der Massenproteste in Bahrain zum Einsatz kam. Dabei ging es aber um innere Unruhen und keine Bedrohung von außen.
Trotz mehrerer Initiativen haben die Golfstaaten bisher kein vollständig integriertes System zur gemeinsamen Verteidigung. Ihnen fehlt eine einheitliche Linie dazu, auf welche Bedrohungen sie gemeinsam reagieren wollen. Auch Fragen zur Führung sind ungeklärt. Die Differenzen wurden vor allem im Konflikt Saudi-Arabiens mit den Emiraten sichtbar. Die Golfstaaten suchen neben dem langjährigen und wichtigsten Partner USA zunehmend auch nach neuen Verbündeten bei der Verteidigung, etwa Pakistan und die Türkei.
Wegen der erneuten Eskalation im Jemen mit der Huthi-Miliz steht derzeit vor allem Saudi-Arabien unter Beschuss. Erst am Montag meldete das Königreich, dass die wichtige Ost-West-Ölpipeline erneut Ziel eines Angriffs geworden sei. Dabei sei ein Feuer ausgebrochen, das inzwischen gelöscht worden sei, berichtete die staatliche Nachrichtenagentur SPA unter Berufung auf einen Vertreter des Ministeriums. Der Angriff sei in der Medina-Region im Westen des Königreichs erfolgt.
Es habe weder Verletzte noch Auswirkungen auf den Betrieb der Pipeline gegeben. Einsatzkräfte und technische Spezialteams hätten unmittelbar nach dem Angriff mit den notwendigen Maßnahmen begonnen, um den Ort des Vorfalls abzusichern, hieß es weiter.
Von wem der Angriff ausging, führte Saudi-Arabien zunächst nicht weiter aus. Das saudische Außenministerium hatte einen vorigen Angriff auf die Pipeline proiranischen Milizen aus dem Irak zugeschrieben.
Die Ost-West-Pipeline, durch die unter Umgehung der faktisch blockierten Straße von Hormus große Mengen Öl vom Persischen Golf zum Roten Meer transportiert werden können, wurde nach Angriffen Mitte September eine Zeit lang stillgelegt. Sie ist aktuell aber wieder in Betrieb.

A17.text:
‘I pay $500 for 5 square metres’: Spain’s protesters, in their own words
Young people are trapped in the family home or forced to pay high rents for cramped accommodation, at the mercy of landlords.
Tens of thousands of young people have protested across Spain in recent weeks, rallying against the country’s acute housing crisis. On Wednesday, many have gone on strike, heeding calls by Spain’s biggest unions for a nationwide walkout under the slogan: “Salarios, vivienda y precios” – or “wages, housing, and prices”.
Anger grew last month after the forcible eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal from the Madrid flat where she had lived for the past seven decades. Her corporate landlord had raised the rent to a level above her means. As the public outcry worsened, she died in hospital the day the property owners who had evicted her agreed to allow her to return to her home.
To protect vulnerable renters, the government presented two emergency decrees to parliament, but these were defeated by right-wing parties.
Spain’s left-wing coalition government called a snap election for November 29, hoping to capitalise on anger over the housing crisis to rally voters as Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez had trailed in the polls to the conservative People’s Party and the far-right Vox party.
Against this backdrop, the Bank of Spain has said the country has a shortage of 750,000 homes, but this figure could rise to 1 million by next year.
Al Jazeera spoke to several protesters about their demands:
‘I still live with my parents as housing is so expensive’
Haris Javaid Sharif, 24, a data analyst, lives with his parents, brother and sister in a 44sq-metre (474-foot) flat in Barcelona. Sharif earns $1,900 per month net. The family pay $745 for their rented flat, of which he pays half. He still lives with his parents as average rental prices for a three-bedroom flat in Barcelona range between $954 and $1,684.
“After the pandemic, we were evicted from our flat because we owed five months rent. My father and I could not work because of the pandemic. When we got the 2,500 euros ($2,800), the owner did not want to negotiate and we lost our home.
“We went 11 months without work and we lived in two-room accommodation. I thought it only happens to vulnerable people, but it can happen to anyone.
“I still live with my parents as housing is so expensive. I am joining the strike to try to press these politicians. The housing problems for youngsters is the biggest problem. I speak to people who don’t see themselves buying a house in 10 years’ time.”
‘We are worried our landlord might kick us out’
Bea Garcia de la Torre, 32, who works for a foundation in Madrid, shares a 70sq-metre (753sq-foot) flat with her brother. They pay $1,229 per month in rent. She earns $2,400 per month.
“I am not in the worst position. There are some people who have to pay half their monthly wages in rent. My brother and I share the rent, but the landlord is trying to get us to pay for the central heating, which is something which should be paid for by the community. We are also worried that he might put up the rent to an astronomical amount or kick us out.
“I will join this general strike because it is a good chance to change the housing policy in this country, just like we did with a similar action and won the right to an eight-hour day.”
‘The landlord could push up the rent or just get rid of us’
Iratxe Gonzalez, 27, a social worker, shares a flat in Madrid with three other people. She earns $1,200 per month, of which she pays $400 in rent for the flat of 45sq metres (484sq foot).
“I needed to leave my parents’ home, but the flat is very small, and we only have a short-term contract of one year. It is not very secure. The landlord could push up the rent or just get rid of us.

A196.text:
Spain’s general strike puts housing crisis at centre of upcoming elections
Millions of Spanish workers are striking Wednesday – the first general strike in 14 years – to demand action on a major housing crisis and the rising cost of living. The expected disruptions to public transport and the widespread closure of businesses come less than three weeks before a snap election that could bring the far right to power.
Millions of Spain’s workers are striking Wednesday to demand that the government remedy the nation’s housing crisis less than three weeks before a national election that could catapult the far right to power.
Spain’s first general strike in 14 years is expected to cause delays to the widely used public transport system and lead to the slowdown or shuttering of businesses, factories and shops across the eurozone’s fourth-largest economy.
Tensions flared at the start of the strike at Madrid's Mercamadrid wholesale market, where about 1,000 protesters gathered. CCOO's Madrid branch said on X that police fired pepper spray at pickets and arrested one of them, with 13 people requiring medical attention.
Minor incidents were reported in the first hours, including roadblocks – some of them with burning tires – in Barcelona, the second-largest city in the country, and scuffles between picketers and police near the country’s main wholesale market on the outskirts of the capital, Madrid. Striking workers set off fireworks on the stroke of midnight as they gathered in public squares in Barcelona.
The two main unions calling for the strike, UGT and CCOO, reported widespread participation in the early hours “with significant work stoppages in strategic sectors” – 90 percent in the automotive and port sectors, 85 percent in the meat industry, 82 percent in waste collection and 75 percent in the energy sector – according to a statement posted on social media.
To display this content from X (Twitter), you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
Between workers, activists, politicians and ordinary Spaniards, the groups have very different interests in Wednesday's walkout.
The average rent in Spain has almost doubled in the last 10 years, eating into household budgets and angering voters.
Spain has a deficit of about 750,000 homes, which is set to grow to more than a million by 2028, according to the central bank.
With fewer people able to afford a home, renting has increased sharply, putting pressure on that market. The average rental price of €1,176 ($1,315) is equivalent to about 98.7 percent of a young person's average monthly salary in Spain, according to the Youth Council of Spain.
"We won't stop until we transform this country's housing model from top to bottom so that houses are for living instead of being at the service of the rentier minority," said Aliciadel Rio, spokesperson for the Madrid Tenants' Union, as the strike began at midnight.
Public anger over housing reached a boiling point following the nationally televised eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her home in Madrid last month. The subsequent death of Maricarmen, as the woman became known, caused even more indignation and solidified her as a symbol of Spaniards who feel they pay too much on rent and can’t even dream of homeownership.
Read moreTens of thousands march in Madrid to mourn pensioner whose eviction sparked housing protests
Housing activists leveraged the uproar over Maricarmen's eviction to call for the general strike. They soon won the backing of Spain's two main unions, UGT and CCOO.
The housing activists want several measures, including the elimination of tourist apartments, a crackdown on real estate speculation and protection for renters in the form of automatic renewals of leases.
The UGT and CCOO unions are demanding more government intervention in the housing market and a new minimum wage agreement through talks with the business owners' association.
The strike’s official slogan is “Salaries. Housing.

A20.text:
Ebola cases in DR Congo pass 11,000, with 5,387 deaths
Authorities struggling to contain DRC’s largest Ebola outbreak due to delated detection, conflict and strained health services.
The number of confirmed Ebola cases in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) has reached 11,042, according to government data, with at least 5,387 deaths.
The figures, released on Tuesday, came as health authorities in the DRC struggle to contain the largest and deadliest Ebola outbreak in the country’s history.
The outbreak is caused by the rare Bundibugyo strain of the Ebola virus.
It is now the second-largest and second-deadliest Ebola outbreak on record, behind only the 2014-2016 West African outbreak. That epidemic infected more than 28,600 people and killed more than 11,000.
Eight of the DRC’s 26 provinces have been affected in the ongoing outbreak, and many deaths have occurred outside treatment centres.
Delayed detection, conflict and strained health services have led to a more rapid spread of the virus than in previous outbreaks.
Containment has been especially difficult because no vaccine or treatment has been developed specifically for the Bundibugyo strain, which kills about half of the people it infects.
Earlier this month, the World Health Organization approved clinical trials of two new Ebola vaccines and said it expected results in early 2027.
Cases have now been reported in East, Central and West Africa, giving it the widest geographic spread of any Ebola outbreak on the continent to date.

A21.text:
Russia, Ukraine exchange strikes as Baltic nations issue drone alerts
Attacks also reported in the Russian-occupied Donbas region of Ukraine as US-mediated talks continue in Abu Dhabi.
Several Baltic nations have issued a flurry of alerts, urging citizens to seek shelter against threats from unidentified drones, as Russia and Ukraine traded attacks.
Ukrainian drones attacked Russia’s northwest, home to major Baltic Sea export facilities and a big oil refinery, setting the Ust-Luga port area on fire and injuring three, the Reuters news agency said on Wednesday.
Drone debris killed two in Russia’s Smolensk region bordering Belarus, Russian newswires reported, quoting the local governor.
In Ukraine, an overnight Russian air strike knocked out power in parts of the industrial stronghold of Kryvyi Rih, injuring one person in Kharkiv, the country’s second-biggest city, and six others in Zaporizhzhia, officials and emergency services said.
Russia’s Ministry of Defence said its forces struck a cargo vessel in the Black Sea southwest of Odesa that was carrying weapons and military equipment for Ukraine’s armed forces.
The ministry also said Russian drones hit three electricity substations in Ukraine’s Kryvyi Rih and Odesa regions overnight.
Meanwhile, the Baltic nations of Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia issued alerts for drones entering from neighbouring Russia or Belarus. Lithuanian crisis officials said the warning covered Kaunas, the country’s second-largest city, home to about 300,000 people.
The alerts said NATO air defence jets had been activated. There were no reports of injuries.
Finland, another Russian neighbour, adopted temporary airspace and maritime curbs in the eastern Gulf of Finland but withdrew them later.
“The restrictions were a precautionary measure to ensure the authorities’ ability to operate and the safety of bystanders,” its defence forces said on X.
The attacks come a day after Russia said it shot down more than 140 drones in an ongoing attack on the country’s Leningrad region northwest of Moscow.
“A total of 146 drones have been downed over the Leningrad Region,” Governor Aleksandr Drozdenko said on Telegram, Russia’s state news agency TASS reported, adding that “the counter-action is ongoing”.
It is unclear where the drones came from, but on Monday, a Ukrainian drone struck Russia’s second-largest oil refinery in Kirishi, also in the Leningrad region, according to Reuters. Local authorities said a woman had been killed in the attack.
‘Constructive’ Abu Dhabi talks
The escalation comes as US-mediated peace talks between Russia and Ukraine in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, entered their second and final day on Wednesday.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the first day of talks was “constructive and quite substantive”.
The attacks in Russia also came as TASS reported that Ukrainian forces had fired at least 31 artillery shells at Ukraine’s Moscow-occupied Donetsk region in 24 hours, wounding three civilians.
Of these attacks, 23 occurred in the Horlivka area, where a couple was also wounded in a drone strike on a vehicle, according to TASS.
Attacks were also reported in Zelenskyy’s hometown of Kryvyi Rih, Ukrainian officials said on Telegram.

A217.text:
Prime Minister Mark Carney and several other world leaders who failed to attend the UN Climate Conference in Turkey have been awarded the “fossil of the day” title.
Climate Action Network International, which has handed out the satirical award since 1999, says Tuesday’s edition went to the “absent leaders of wealthy countries,” including Canada, Germany, France, Japan and Denmark.
“Despite widespread public demands for stronger climate action, these countries’ empty chairs send a dismal signal about their commitment to international climate co-operation,” said a Climate Action Network International press release.
“They haven’t gone as far as the United States in abandoning the Paris Agreement altogether, but they appear to have decided that COP31 is no longer important enough to warrant their presence.”
The press release said the leaders’ summit is where heads of government set political direction, build alliances and “earn the trust that unlocks progress in the negotiations.”
“It is also where they can sit down with their peers from vulnerable countries and hear their priorities first-hand,” it said. “With multilateral co-operation under growing strain, that matters more than ever.”
Opinion: The climate energy transition was a broken promise
Canada’s reputation as a global climate leader took a hit last year when it was awarded the “fossil of the day” award at the UN Climate Conference in Brazil.
At the time, Climate Action Network International said Canada was singled out for the first time in more than a decade for “flushing years of climate action down the drain.”
New Zealand received the award on Monday, as Climate Action Network International said its government has dismantled its climate commitments by gutting methane targets and changing the law to shield corporations from climate litigation.
Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin is attending the first week of the conference and some climate activists say Canada can expect some criticism there from other nations over its recent climate policy shifts.

Climate crisis is 'outrunning us', UN chief warns COP31
By Tuvan Gumrukcu and Valerie Volcovici
ANTALYA, Turkey, Nov 11 (Reuters) - UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres told world leaders at the COP31 summit in Turkey on Wednesday that the slow international response to climate change so far had placed the world on a path to destruction.
Governments must fight harder to preserve the planet for future generations, he said, in comments that set the tone for two days of rapid-fire speeches by world leaders at the UN conference on Turkey's Mediterranean coast.
"The brutal truth is that the climate crisis is outrunning us. This is the path to mutually assured destruction," Guterres said, pointing to rising emissions, global temperatures and worsening climate-driven disasters.
"But science is not telling us to surrender. It is telling us to fight harder."
Negotiators from nearly 200 countries are seeking agreement on a plan to increase the share of electricity in global energy use and revive stalled efforts to move away from fossil fuels.
The summit opened on Monday against the backdrop of wars, rampant inflation and other crises that are competing for political attention – but also amid increasingly alarming signals about the pace of global warming.
YEAR OF EXTREME WEATHER
A UN report last month found the world on course to break through the 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) warming limit that countries had agreed to pursue under the Paris Agreement to prevent the worst effects of climate change.
Meanwhile, 2026 has also stood out with a series of extreme heatwaves across Western Europe and a glacier collapse in Nepal that triggered a catastrophic flood killing more than 1,450 people, with thousands still missing.
Former French Prime Minister Laurent Fabius, who presided over the 2015 Paris climate conference and leads an advisory council of former COP presidents, said on Tuesday the leaders' speeches should give political impetus to the negotiations.
"It is an opportunity for leaders to make some announcements, and more this time, to explain how they will implement, because the key word in Antalya is implementation," he told Reuters.
Wednesday's speakers are expected to include Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who was re-elected at the end of October, and whose country hosted last year's climate talks. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, Chinese Vice President Han Zheng, and Marshall Islands President Hilda Heine will also speak.
The United States, the world's largest historical emitter of greenhouse gases, has skipped the talks for the second year in a row after President Donald Trump – who has called global warming a hoax – withdrew the US from climate cooperation following his return to office in 2025.
Several other nations, including France, Germany, Japan, Italy and Canada, did not send their top leaders to the talks this year and won't be represented in the speeches.
"The world's biggest economies should be leading the response to the climate crisis, not leaving it to others," said Mohamed Adow, director of climate and energy think tank, Power Shift Africa.
AGE OF ELECTRICITY?
COP31 host Turkey has been pushing for countries to put a goal on electrification at the centre of a final deal, though critics say it may do little to curb warming.
The proposal targets a rise in electricity's share of total global energy consumption to 35% by 2035, up from a little over a fifth now, theoretically reducing greenhouse gas emissions from cars, factories and buildings.
But the proposal does not include language requiring new power to be generated by clean energy sources, and governments have yet to clarify a broader plan to transition away from fossil fuels like coal, oil and gas.
Guterres urged countries to speed their transition to clean energy sources.

A307.text:
Spain's first general strike in 14 years demands solutions to housing crisis
BARCELONA, Spain — Less than three weeks before a national election that could catapult the far right to power, millions of Spain's workers are striking on Wednesday to demand that the government remedy the nation's housing crisis.
The general strike — Spain's first in 14 years — is causing delays in the public transport system and slowing down factories across the eurozone's fourth-largest economy. Many schools and universities reportedly closed or are working at minimal capacity. In the capital, Madrid, this adds to an ongoing strike started by teachers nearly a month ago to demand better working conditions.
In Barcelona, the country's second-largest city, public transport was at a standstill or facing long delays in the morning rush hour. In Madrid, which saw heavy rains in the morning, city buses were the hardest affected. Unions have called for Madrid workers to gather and march through the city center later Wednesday. Marches and gatherings are also planned in Barcelona and other cities.
The two main unions calling for the strike, UGT and CCOO, said in a statement that there was widespread participation, "with significant work stoppages in strategic sectors" — 90% in the automotive and port sectors, 85% in the meat industry, 82% in waste collection, and 75% in the energy sector.
"It's extremely important to remind people that we, the workers — who are also renters or who also pay mortgages — are the ones with the power to halt production and bring the economy to a standstill," Sandra Mora, spokesperson for the Tenants' Union, told the national radio, RNE.
Minor incidents were reported in the first hours of the strike, including roadblocks — some with burning tires — in Barcelona, and scuffles between picketers and police near the country's main wholesale market on Madrid's outskirts.
Earlier, at the stroke of midnight on Wednesday, striking workers set off fireworks as they gathered in public squares in Barcelona.
Workers and activists want more government action on housing
Wednesday's walkout has brought together workers, activists, politicians and ordinary Spaniards around the same interests — accessible housing. The average rent in Spain has almost doubled in the last 10 years, eating into household budgets and angering voters.
"There is one issue that is dividing the country: the struggle to access housing," said Unai Sordo, secretary general of CCOO, on Cadena Ser radio.
Public anger over housing reached a boiling point following the nationally televised eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her home in Madrid last month. The subsequent death of Maricarmen, as the woman became known, caused even more indignation and solidified her as a symbol of Spaniards who feel they pay too much in rent and can't even dream of homeownership.
Housing activists leveraged the uproar over Maricarmen's eviction to call for the general strike. They soon won the backing of the UGT and CCOO unions.
The housing activists want several measures, including the elimination of tourist apartments, a crackdown on real estate speculation and protection for renters in the form of automatic renewals of leases.
The UGT and CCOO unions are demanding more government intervention in the housing market and a new minimum wage agreement through talks with the business owners' association.
Spain's left hopes to put focus back on housing
The nationwide protests over the eviction of Maricarmen propelled Spain's government to push through emergency measures to limit evictions and help tenants, but right-wing parties in the Parliament refused to ratify them on the grounds they would provoke a flight of properties from the rental market.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez responded by doubling down politically and called the election on Oct. 5, hoping to earn four more years in power for his left-wing coalition.

A308.text:
Ebola tops 11,000 cases in Congo's deadliest outbreak
BUNIA, Congo — Congo's Ebola outbreak has topped 11,000 cases, the government said Wednesday, a stark figure that underscores the severity of the situation as the country grapples with the relentless spread of the disease.
According to the latest health ministry data, 11,042 people have been infected with the deadly virus that has now killed 5,387 — nearly half of those infected in what has been Congo's deadliest outbreak.
The outbreak was declared in mid-May, and since then, Congolese authorities have struggled to contain it due to several factors, including armed conflicts, a health system crisis, poor roads and violence from residents fueled by mistrust and misinformation.
The Bundibugyo virus responsible for this outbreak has no known vaccine or treatment and has spread to eight of the country's 26 provinces.
The resurgence of violence in the two major hotspots in Ituri and North Kivu provinces has sparked worry among health authorities who are calling for a halt to the fighting to allow health workers unhindered access to the sick.
Health facilities and medical professionals have also been targeted by many in communities skeptical of the virus, and there have been several attacks on health workers.
Experts have called for more efforts to slow and contain the disease in Congo, while it has spread to multiple African countries including Uganda, Kenya and Nigeria.
Dozens of Ebola outbreaks have been reported since the disease was first discovered in 1976. The largest and deadliest occurred in West Africa in 2014 to 2016, with 28,000 infections and more than 11,000 deaths.
The current outbreak already ranks second and has had at least three times the number of cases and deaths in the time since it was declared, compared with the West Africa outbreak.

A34.text:
US charges three 'Iranian operatives' over UK airbase plot
The US Justice Department on Tuesday announced charges against three men it described as "Iranian operatives," including one already in jail, over their role in an alleged terrorist plot at Britain's RAF Fairford airbase.
Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi, Mohsen Mohajeri and Mohammad Ali al-Hassani allegedly helped plan and direct the September incident at the base, which has been used by the US military in its operations against Iran.
Police were called to the Fairford site in southwest England after a local farmer reported seeing a group of men with several white vans engaged in "suspicious" activity.
A US charging document states that Al-Hassani, a 35-year-old Iraqi national, directed unnamed individuals to drive to the base in the vans, some of which contained barrels of fuel.
It claims that he earlier paid the group to buy metallic objects that could be used as shrapnel, and to disguise the vehicles as being engaged in fuel delivery services.
Al-Saadi, 32, a dual Iranian-Iraqi national already jailed in New York on terrorism charges, allegedly passed coded messages to Al-Hassani and Mohajeri, 48, an Iranian national, to coordinate ahead of the plot.
Days after the incident, the United States withdrew all its B-1 bombers from the base.
"Anyone who plans a terrorist plot on a military base housing American servicemembers will be prosecuted by the United States government," Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a statement Tuesday.
The trio were charged in an eight-count indictment that alleges their involvement in several other plots in support of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and pro-Iranian group Kataeb Hezbollah.
- Terrorist attacks -
US authorities first detailed charges in May against Al-Saadi, accusing him of directing and urging others to attack US and Israeli interests, and to kill Americans and Jews, in retaliation for the US-Israeli war against Iran.
He and associates were said to have planned, coordinated and claimed responsibility for at least 18 terrorist attacks in Europe, and two in Canada.
Examples included the non-fatal stabbing of two Jewish men in London in April, as well as several arson attacks on synagogues, Israeli businesses and Jewish schools in Amsterdam, Munich and elsewhere.
Al-Saadi has been in US custody since May.
The latest indictment adds his apparent role in the RAF Fairford incident, as well as the alleged involvement of Al-Hassani and Mohajeri. Prosecutors did not disclose their whereabouts.
The three men are charged with conspiracy to provide material support to terrorist groups Kataeb Hezbollah and the IRGC, conspiring and providing material support for acts of terrorism, and conspiring to bomb a place of public use.
Al-Saadi is additionally charged with attempted acts of terrorism transcending national boundaries, and attempted destruction of property by means of fire or explosive.
UK police last month charged two British men with national security offenses related to the RAF Fairford incident.
One was charged with assisting a foreign intelligence service, believed to be in Iran, and another with entering a prohibited place for a purpose "prejudicial" to the UK.
Flight-tracking data showed on Tuesday that the US military had removed at least a dozen aircraft from a second British airbase, RAF Mildenhall, following what the Wall Street Journal said was a threat from Iran.

A53.text:
The investigation of Jensen Huang by Nvidia’s board threatens the future of one of Silicon Valley’s longest-serving executives and a key enabler of the AI boom, who has no obvious successor as leader of the world’s second-most-valuable company.
Huang is fighting for survival after admitting to an extramarital affair, believed to be with an executive at a large Nvidia customer whom US officials also allege was working as a Chinese spy.
The prospect that Huang could be forced out as chief executive of the US chipmaker he co-founded more than 30 years ago has alarmed investors and allies in the tech industry. Shares in Nvidia, which late last month ceded its position as the world’s most valuable to Apple amid a broader sell-off in AI stocks, had fallen more than 5 percent by midday trading on Monday.
“Jensen is irreplaceable for America’s AI leadership,” said Shaun Maguire, partner at early Nvidia investor Sequoia Capital, in a social media post.
Nvidia’s chips were instrumental in the creation of generative AI tools such as ChatGPT and now sit at the center of Big Tech’s $1 trillion AI infrastructure frenzy. Huang has personally stood behind investments and guarantees running into hundreds of billions of dollars for dozens of AI start-ups and data center providers, as well as lobbying US President Donald Trump for looser AI regulation.
“Nvidia is not an ordinary company and Jensen is not an ordinary CEO; he IS Nvidia,” analysts at Bernstein said in a note to clients.
With policymakers in Washington pressuring Huang to appear before congressional committees to explain himself, the spotlight is on Nvidia’s board, which said on Sunday it would conduct its own “independent” investigation into the scandal that exploded over the weekend.
The investigation will probably be led by board member and former Cooley chief executive Stephen C. Neal, according to people familiar with the probe.
“If information was compromised, the implications are a lot bigger than if it was just an affair, which obviously isn’t welcome news,” said a fund manager with a large Nvidia position. “Nvidia would survive [Huang leaving] but there’s no better person than Jensen to run the company; it would be very different without him.”
In contrast to other leading Big Tech companies, Nvidia’s annual reports and corporate governance paperwork make no specific reference to “succession planning” and set out no details for how it would replace its CEO, even in an emergency, beyond noting that the company “believe[s] in extensive leadership development.”
Huang’s unusually large number of direct reports, numbered at more than 60 according to a 2024 disclosure, present Nvidia’s board with a “pool of excellent candidates for future promotion,” recent filings say.
Huang leads a small core executive team at Nvidia, including Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress, Operations Chief Debora Shoquist and general counsel Tim Teter. He has become one of Huang’s closest lieutenants since joining in 2017 and has lobbied Washington on export controls.
Jay Puri, a close lieutenant who led Nvidia’s sales operations and deputized for Huang on international visits, stepped down in August and was replaced on the executive team by Microsoft veteran Nick Parker.
Huang, who has cultivated an air of infallibility inside Nvidia, has given no indication he will step down from the role of CEO.
Recent biographies of Huang and Nvidia, including Tae Kim’s The Nvidia Way and Stephen Witt’s The Thinking Machine, portray him as having a rare combination of technical depth and forward-thinking leadership.
He is known to be able to inspire extraordinary productivity inside a company whose 42,000 employees each generated an average of more than $7 million in annual revenue over the past 12 months, far more than any other Big Tech group. But Kim also notes that Huang represents the company’s “single point of failure,” functioning as its head of marketing, sales, and product development.

A6.text:
Putin is not ready to make peace in Abu Dhabi
The humanitarian breakthrough in Oleshky has not changed Moscow’s calculations. Putin believes he can outlast Western support for Ukraine.
As the Russian-Ukrainian war, which long ago entered a phase of attrition, grinds on, Russia, Ukraine and the United States began a new round of US-brokered trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates, on November 10. The talks are scheduled to continue on November 11.
The talks follow a successful humanitarian operation in Oleshky, a southern Ukrainian town that has been occupied by Russian forces since 2022.
Starting in December 2025, Oleshky experienced a food crisis that worsened dramatically in the summer of this year. Over the years under Russian occupation, its population declined from 25,000 to 2,000 people, and the food crisis threatened the survival of those who remained. In the summer, however, Ukrainian and Russian intelligence services agreed to work on a local ceasefire in order to evacuate Oleshky’s inhabitants – if they wanted to leave – either to Ukraine or to Russia.
The humanitarian mission went surprisingly smoothly. Both sides stood by the ceasefire agreement, hundreds of people were successfully evacuated (mostly to Ukraine) from the long-suffering town, and it was extraordinary to see the Ukrainian and Russian human rights representatives, Dmytro Lubinets and Yana Lantratova, coordinating the humanitarian mission peacefully and with mutual respect.
Can this successful mission lay the groundwork for – or at least contribute to – progress in the Abu Dhabi peace negotiations brokered by the US between Russia and Ukraine? Several factors suggest that this is unlikely.
One immediate indicator is that the success of the mission in Oleshky was driven not by Moscow’s desire for peace but by its willingness to pander to Donald Trump’s vanity against the background of his animosity towards Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
It has long been known that Trump wanted to be awarded the Nobel Peace Prize. However, despite his claims that he has ended countless wars around the world, Trump is unlikely to receive this prestigious award. Today, it seems that the Trump family’s plan is to try to secure the Nobel Peace Prize for Melania Trump.
The Oleshky humanitarian mission seems to be a case in point. A few days before the ceasefire, the White House announced that it was Melania Trump – in “her formal role as Exclusive Intermediary” – who had initiated discussions on the ceasefire agreement between Russia and Ukraine, thus dismissing not only the Vatican’s efforts to secure the Oleshky ceasefire, but also the fact that Ukrainian and Russian intelligence services had already begun discussing the temporary armistice in the summer. Moscow, however, readily backed Washington’s version of Melania Trump’s critical role in the agreement, and Kyiv had to align with that version, too.
Both Russia and Ukraine are seeking to win Donald Trump over to their side, but while both countries eventually agreed to play along with the White House’s promotion of the US first lady as a “peacemaker”, Moscow presumably considered that the success of the Oleshky humanitarian mission would benefit it more than Kyiv. Putin’s apparent reasoning here is that Moscow’s apparent willingness to cooperate may deepen Trump’s disaffection with Zelenskyy and strengthen his delusion that it is Ukraine rather than Russia that is blocking the path to the end of the war. For Putin, winning Trump over would be a way to continue the aggression against Ukraine under more favourable circumstances – not a way to come to peace with Ukraine.
Another factor suggesting that the Abu Dhabi talks are unlikely to result in progress towards lasting peace is that Moscow appointed Vladimir Medinsky, Putin’s aide, as the head of the Russian delegation for the talks in the UAE.

Section one of the Act relates to obtaining or disclosing protected information, while section three relates to assisting a foreign intelligence service.

US warns Madagascar over growing military ties with Russia
- Published
The US has warned Madagascar against strengthening its ties with Russia, saying similar partnerships with military-led governments in West Africa have failed to improve security.
US Africa Command deputy head Lt Gen John Brennan said Madagascar's strategic location in the Indian Ocean made it important to global trade.
He warned against what he called the "Sahel model", which he said risked fuelling instability across the continent.
Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger, all under military rule, have severed ties with the Western partners and turned to Russia to military support their fight against jihadist groups.
Russia has expanded its military cooperation with Madagascar since the military seized power in 2025, supplying weapons and military instructors.
"We are concerned about Russia wanting to "proliferate [the Sahel model] elsewhere across the continent", Brennan told reporters in an online briefing.
"Madagascar sits in a location that is extremely important, as is Mozambique, and we don't want to see those models be applied in those two locations," he said.
The three Sahel countries had blamed their former Western partners for failing to contain jihadist violence before turning to Moscow.
However, militant attacks have continued despite their closer military ties with Russia.
Brennan also raised concerns about security in the Mozambique Channel, which separates Mozambique and Madagascar from mainland Africa and is an important route for international shipping and trade.
He said it was vital to prevent Islamist State linked militants in northern Mozambique and other hostile actors from threatening maritime activity.
Citing recent piracy-related incidents along the coast, Brennan said militant groups in northern Mozambique were adapting their tactics, including developing greater maritime capabilities.
He said US partners were "free to partner with whom they wish" but urged them to understand the potential risks.
Madagascar has not publicly responded to Brennan's comments,.
However, President Michaël Randrianirina has recently reiterated his support for stronger ties between Russia and African countries.
During the Russia-Africa summit last month, Madagascar and Russia signed several cooperation agreements covering defence, tourism and trade.
In February, a few months after taking power in a military takeover, Randrianirina visited to Moscow. It was the first official visit to Russia by a Malagasy leader in nearly 50 years.

Who is Alice Huang? Alleged Chinese spy, businesswoman involved with Nvidia CEO
Independent board investigation, FBI inquiry underway after Huang accused of spying for Beijing
Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang has been thrust into the spotlight for being involved with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.
But little public information is available about the woman accused by U.S. officials of being a spy for Beijing by collecting intelligence from one of the world’s most valuable tech giants.
The two, who are not related, have been photographed at multiple events together.
The New York Times reported last month that U.S. authorities had concluded she was a Chinese intelligence asset who passed information to Beijing while developing a close relationship with the Nvidia CEO, believed to be targeted by a foreign intelligence effort.
Reuters could not independently verify the intelligence allegation, which China has denied. Reuters could not determine Alice Huang's whereabouts to seek comment.
Here’s what we know about the Chinese businesswoman accused of espionage.
From TV journalist to finance to AI chips
Alice Huang built a career in Chinese finance before emerging in a very different arena: the global race for artificial intelligence chips.
Known also as Huang Le, the Chinese businesswoman held senior roles at a Shanghai investment firm before becoming the controlling shareholder of Singapore-based cloud-computing company Megaspeed International, according to more than 30 publicly available financial records, corporate filings and company materials reviewed by Reuters.
Nvidia lists Megaspeed as an official cloud partner on its directory. Megaspeed attracted public attention in October 2025, when the New York Times reported the company was under U.S. investigation over whether it was helping Chinese customers obtain advanced Nvidia chips subject to Washington's export controls.

Alice Huang, reported by Chinese financial publication Caixin to be about 42 years old, previously worked in banking and investment management, according to Chinese fund-industry records and an indexed profile on private-fund database Simuwang, which also listed an earlier career in television journalism.
Before her involvement with Megaspeed, she held senior positions at Shanghai Hexi Investment Management, a Chinese investment firm.
Several posts on Hexi's official WeChat account between 2016 and 2017 identified her as the firm's deputy general manager, executive director and a member of its investment decision committee and said she had previously worked at HSBC's private bank in Hong Kong and at CITIC Securities. HSBC and CITIC did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
A Hexi business card reviewed by Reuters identified Alice Huang as a partner and general manager, with an office in Shanghai's Lujiazui financial district. At the Aurora Plaza address listed on the card, Reuters found offices undergoing extensive renovation, with no Hexi signage or staff present. Calls to a number on the card went unanswered, and an email address could not receive messages.
Huang became Megaspeed's controlling shareholder in March 2023, according to Washington-based research group C4ADS, which reviewed corporate records. Incorporated in Singapore in 2015 as 7Road International, Megaspeed provides cloud-computing services and describes itself on its company website as an Nvidia business partner in the Asia-Pacific region.
Huang also served as a director and managing director of Megaspeed's Indonesian subsidiary from March to November 2023, C4ADS said. Megaspeed did not respond to a request for comment.

Unnamed 41-year-old arrested near Gloucester
A member of the U.S. Army assigned to a NATO unit was arrested Tuesday in England on suspicion of espionage related to Russia, counterterror police and other officials said.

He was serving in NATO's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps at Imjin Barracks near Gloucester, according to a U.S. official, a senior NATO official and a British government official. The man is an officer, the U.S. official said. All three spoke to The Associated Press on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive military matters.
The Allied Rapid Reaction Corps is a multinational land unit within the NATO military alliance that is designed to quickly respond to crises or short-notice operations. According to the unit's website, it is made up of forces from 20 nations — including from Canada — but is led by the British and based in Gloucester, where the U.S. soldier was arrested.

Carney selects new ambassador to China, plans to announce 'in very short order'
Canada without a permanent ambassador in Beijing since April
Canadians will know the name of their new ambassador to China "in very short order," said Prime Minister Mark Carney on Tuesday.
The position has been unfilled for six months.
"It's a little longer than we would have liked," Carney said at a news conference in Montreal. "We wanted to get the right person and we have found that right person."
He said the standard formal diplomatic process is underway to have China, the host country, approve the proposed candidate.
Jennifer May served as Canada's last ambassador to China, stepping down from her role in April to become Carney's foreign and defence policy adviser in the Privy Council Office.
She was Canada's first female ambassador to the People's Republic of China, and had been appointed to the role in September 2022.
"As I leave Beijing, I do so with deep gratitude for the experiences, partnerships and friendships built here, and with anticipation for the challenges ahead," May said in a LinkedIn post earlier this year.
"I am proud of the work we've done to navigate complex realities, advance Canada's interests, support Canadian businesses and deliver new priorities under a new government."
Carney in China next week
The announcement comes ahead of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation's (APEC) leaders' summit in China next week, which Carney is expected to attend from Nov. 18 to 19.
There, Carney says he and Chinese President Xi Jinping will discuss several topics including global security and the two countries' economic partnership, which he described as "something that is deepening, but has clear guardrails in terms of the areas in which we're involved."
"The advantage of these meetings is that you can raise issues directly and frankly and I will be raising the importance with which we attach to the non-interference in our affairs by China and other countries," Carney said.

A89.text:

Anthropic eyes $1 trillion US valuation in hotly anticipated IPO that's a key test for AI market
Anthropic's stock offering could set a benchmark for the AI sector
Anthropic's blockbuster initial public offering (IPO) is set to give the company a valuation of up to $1.4 trillion US, slightly lower than some investors' expectations amid a recent cooling in investor appetite for AI, setting up a defining test of Wall Street's faith in the boom that it helped ignite.
The AI lab best known for its Claude chatbot, along with some of its investors, is aiming to raise up to $64.4 billion US by selling 825 million shares in the IPO priced up to $78 US per share.
Anthropic will also raise $26 billion US via a separate private placement deal with cornerstone investors such as Alphabet's Google, Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices.
The company is launching the roadshow for a historic share sale that is expected to set a benchmark for the sector following years of hype that fuelled a massive influx of capital into AI companies.
"What we are seeing is essentially a reassessment of Anthropic's value in a more challenging AI environment," said Ipek Ozkardeskaya, senior analyst at Swissquote Bank in Geneva. "The company continues to post impressive growth, but investors are increasingly focused on the cost of generating that growth."
At the top of the price range, Anthropic would be valued at about $1.4 trillion US on a fully diluted basis, which includes securities such as stock options and restricted stock. On a non-diluted basis, excluding those securities, the company’s market value would be about $1 trillion.
Hours before Anthropic filed an updated prospectus with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) on Tuesday, details of its IPO, including the proposed price range, were briefly circulated to investment banks late on Monday shortly before being retracted, according to emails seen by Reuters.
The preliminary terms showed Anthropic planned to sell about 867 million shares at up to $80 US apiece in an offering that could raise as much as $69.3 billion US, including shares sold by existing shareholders.
The prospectus ultimately filed with the SEC contained different terms, with Anthropic setting a lower price range and targeting reduced proceeds.
Big spend concerns
Nvidia joined the deal amid an FBI probe into its CEO Jensen Huang's affair with a Chinese woman alleged to be a spy for Beijing, which has also triggered an internal investigation.
Investors had previously discussed a valuation of as much as $2 trillion US, but expectations have since come down given the company's substantial infrastructure commitments and the recent volatility in AI-related stocks, with the $1.5 trillion US figure viewed as the high end of the range, Reuters previously reported.
"The shift from a $2 trillion US valuation to today's level reflects a change in focus from revenue growth alone to the significant financial commitments and spending required to sustain it," Ozkardeskaya said.
Investors are also closely watching Anthropic’s IPO for clues about rival OpenAI, which is seeking to raise $30 billion US in what is expected to be its final private funding round before a potential IPO early next year. OpenAI recently secured $11 billion US at a $1.25 trillion US valuation, below the $1.5 trillion it had initially sought.
The second half of the year has brought a reckoning for the AI boom, as investors question whether returns will justify the massive spending and mounting debt costs in an elevated interest-rate environment. Concerns are also rising over the sustainability of the investment cycle, with questions around circular financing arrangements, the risk of infrastructure overcapacity and how quickly companies can turn their AI investments into revenue.

A9.text:
Iran denies talks with US, says Hormuz will stay shut until demands are met
Mohsen Rezaei’s comments come as the IRGC said at least three ships had hit mines and caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz.
Rubio says no need for major combat operations against Iran
Iran’s security chief Mohsen Rezaei has said that Tehran is waiting for a response from the United States on its seven conditions for peace talks, while dismissing speculation about holding any negotiations with Washington.
Rezaei’s comments on Tuesday came as hopes grow for a diplomatic breakthrough in the US and Israel’s war on Iran after US President Donald Trump said that he saw “positive momentum” towards ending the conflict.
Trump, who held talks with Qatar’s Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani at the White House on Monday, also said that new attacks on Iran were unnecessary. Qatar is a key mediator in the conflict.
Rezaei told Lebanon’s Al Mayadeen TV on Tuesday that claims “about continuing negotiations or holding a meeting in Qatar is a pure lie”, saying that Washington was talking up negotiations to ease economic pressure and bring down oil prices.
He said the Strait of Hormuz – the global maritime corridor that Iran closed – will not reopen until the US meets Tehran’s seven conditions. “Their initial response was insufficient and deceptive, and we are still waiting for an explicit and clear response,” he said.
Iran has not released the full list of conditions. But Rezaei and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi have said it includes lifting sanctions and the US naval blockade, and ending the fighting on all fronts, especially Israel’s attacks on Lebanon.
Araghchi has said that Hormuz could be reopened within two days if the demands are met.
“The conflict with Iran will not be resolved through military means, nor by intensifying sanctions,” Araghchi told the state news agency IRNA on Tuesday. “The only solution is to adopt a language of respect, engage in diplomacy, and address Iran’s demands and conditions – which were outlined in the two-day proposal and remain on the table,” he said.
The war, which is now in its ninth month, has roiled global markets and disrupted oil and gas supplies, pushing up prices around the world.
In the French capital, Paris, where foreign ministers from the Group of 7 were meeting, Sheikh Mohammed held talks with the Saudi foreign minister and four top European diplomats only hours after his meeting with Trump. The French Foreign Ministry said the talks would focus on the Iran crisis and its security and economic fallout.
Speaking to reporters in Paris, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Washington was “open to diplomacy”. He reiterated Trump’s position that further strikes were not needed “if we’re achieving the same objectives through economic means”.
“The economic campaign is so devastating that right now there is no need for major combat operations,” Rubio said. “That’s what I told our allies here today.”
In the Strait of Hormuz, meanwhile, attacks on vessels continued.
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) claimed that three oil tankers caught fire on Tuesday after striking naval mines while transiting an “unauthorised route” in the eastern part of the strait.
The UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency said it received reports of incidents involving two tankers in the region. It said one of the tankers had been struck by an unknown projectile northeast of Oman’s Lima village.
The attacks came after maritime monitoring firms reported at least 37 attacks on ships in and near the Strait of Hormuz in November. The figure is the highest monthly total for ship attacks since the start of the war.

US charges three 'Iranian operatives' over terror plot at UK Fairford airbase
The US Justice Department on Tuesday charged three men it described as Iranian operatives over an alleged September terrorist plot at Britain's RAF Fairford airbase in England. Prosecutors said one suspect directed individuals to drive vans, some carrying fuel barrels, to the base, which housed US military aircraft and personnel.
The US Justice Department on Tuesday announced charges against three men it described as "Iranian operatives", including one already in jail, over their role in an alleged terrorist plot at Britain's RAF Fairford airbase.
Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi, Mohsen Mohajeri and Mohammad Ali al-Hassani allegedly helped plan and direct the September incident at the base, which has been used by the US military in its operations against Iran.
Police were called to the Fairford site in southwest England after a local farmer reported seeing a group of men with several white vans engaged in "suspicious" activity.
A US charging document states that Al-Hassani, a 35-year-old Iraqi national, directed unnamed individuals to drive to the base in the vans, some of which contained barrels of fuel.
It claims that he earlier paid the group to buy metallic objects that could be used as shrapnel, and to disguise the vehicles as being engaged in fuel delivery services.
Al-Saadi, 32, a dual Iranian-Iraqi national already jailed in New York on terrorism charges, allegedly passed coded messages to Al-Hassani and Mohajeri, 48, an Iranian national, to coordinate ahead of the plot.
Days after the incident, the United States withdrew all its B-1 bombers from the base.
"Anyone who plans a terrorist plot on a military base housing American servicemembers will be prosecuted by the United States government," Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a statement Tuesday.
The trio were charged in an eight-count indictment that alleges their involvement in several other plots in support of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and pro-Iranian group Kataeb Hezbollah.
Read moreUS withdraws B-1 bombers from British military base RAF Fairford amid security concerns
Terrorist attacks
US authorities first detailed charges in May against Al-Saadi, accusing him of directing and urging others to attack US and Israeli interests, and to kill Americans and Jews, in retaliation for the US-Israeli war against Iran.
He and associates were said to have planned, coordinated and claimed responsibility for at least 18 terrorist attacks in Europe, and two in Canada.
Examples included the non-fatal stabbing of two Jewish men in London in April, as well as several arson attacks on synagogues, Israeli businesses and Jewish schools in Amsterdam, Munich and elsewhere.
Al-Saadi has been in US custody since May.
The latest indictment adds his apparent role in the RAF Fairford incident, as well as the alleged involvement of Al-Hassani and Mohajeri. Prosecutors did not disclose their whereabouts.
The three men are charged with conspiracy to provide material support to terrorist groups Kataeb Hezbollah and the IRGC, conspiring and providing material support for acts of terrorism, and conspiring to bomb a place of public use.
Al-Saadi is additionally charged with attempted acts of terrorism transcending national boundaries, and attempted destruction of property by means of fire or explosive.
UK police last month charged two British men with national security offenses related to the RAF Fairford incident.
One was charged with assisting a foreign intelligence service, believed to be in Iran, and another with entering a prohibited place for a purpose "prejudicial" to the UK.
Flight-tracking data showed on Tuesday that the US military had removed at least a dozen aircraft from a second British airbase, RAF Mildenhall, following what the Wall Street Journal said was a threat from Iran.

Three men, including one already jailed in the United States, were accused by U.S. authorities Tuesday of being Iran-supported operatives who plotted nearly 20 attacks on Jewish communities in Europe and the U.S. as well as a planned assault on a British airbase used by the U.S. Air Force.
Charges against Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi, a dual Iranian-Iraqi national; Mohsen Mohajeri, an Iranian national; and Mohammad Ali al-Hassani, an Iraqi national, were outlined in a superseding indictment unsealed in Manhattan federal court. Only al-Saadi is in custody.
U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald in New York said in a news release that al-Saadi, who was arrested in the spring, continued to co-ordinate with his co-defendants in the days leading up to the attempted September terrorist plot at a British Royal Air Force Base in Fairford, United Kingdom, where U.S. bombers and troops had been stationed.
“These defendants helped orchestrate a campaign of terror on behalf of terrorist organizations affiliated with Iran that targeted Jewish communities in Europe and the United States, and the British military base, RAF Fairford, housing American service members,” McDonald said. “The threat presented by Iran and Iran-backed terrorist groups to America and our allies is not hypothetical – it is very real.”
U.S. evacuates aircraft from base in England because of threat related to Iran
Attorney-General Todd Blanche said: “Anyone who plans a terrorist plot on a military base housing American servicemembers will be prosecuted by the United States government.”
The new indictment offers fresh insight into an episode that has been shrouded in mystery for more than a month after five men were detained after midnight on Sept. 27 on suspected explosives and terrorism offences after three suspicious vans were spotted travelling toward the base in western England.
A sixth suspect, a British-Iranian dual national, was arrested several days later. All the men were released on bail.
British authorities linked the incident to Tehran, and though Iran denied involvement, the arrests prompted the U.S. to withdraw its bombers that had been stationed there. The bombers were redeployed to their home bases in the United States.
RAF Fairford, located 160 kilometres west of London, has been used by American bombers during decades of conflicts in the Middle East.
According to the indictment, al-Saadi used coded language in communications with relatives from jail to direct that money be passed along to others who could carry out attacks.
U.S. soldier arrested in U.K. on suspicion of assisting Russian intelligence
The indictment alleged that the three men conspired together to use a network of contacts in the United Kingdom to commit terrorist attacks on behalf of an Iran-aligned terrorist network, which included the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and Kata’ib Hizballah.
In June, al-Saadi pleaded not guilty to charges that he plotted at least 18 attacks in Europe in retaliation for the U.S. and Israel’s war with Iran. He called himself a “prisoner of war.” He has been held without bail since. His lawyers did not immediately respond to requests for comment Tuesday on the latest development.
Both Kata’ib Hizballah and Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps have been designated by the U.S. government as foreign terrorist organizations. U.S. prosecutors say Al-Saadi was a Kata’ib Hizballah commander.

A225.text:
A senior U.S. Army soldier was arrested in Britain on suspicion of assisting Russian intelligence, British police said on Tuesday, after the U.S. removed aircraft from British military bases over a separate apparent threat from Iran.
FBI Director Kash Patel said the arrest of the 41-year-old man related to “allegations of espionage, which is of the utmost concern to the United States and our allies.”
Brigadier-general Sean Stinchon, the commanding general of U.S. Army Counterintelligence Command, added: “The alleged conduct of a senior soldier, entrusted with sensitive information, is a sobering reminder that insider threats are real and persistent.”
U.S. evacuates aircraft from base in England because of threat related to Iran
The arrest, which took place near the city of Gloucester, west England, on Tuesday “is not linked to any other ongoing Counter Terrorism Policing investigations,” British police said.
But it occurred the day after the U.S. removed refuelling aircraft from a British airbase in the second such apparent evacuation in three months.
Planes left the Royal Air Force base in Mildenhall, eastern England on Monday which, according to the Wall Street Journal, was prompted by a threat from Iran.
The U.S. in September withdrew bombers that had been used to strike Iran from RAF Fairford on security grounds over an incident police have linked to Iran, which has denied any links to attacks or incidents in Britain.
The U.S. Army soldier arrested on Tuesday was detained on suspicion of offences under sections 1 and 3 of the National Security Act, which relate to obtaining or disclosing protected information and assisting a foreign intelligence service. Police said the country to which the allegations relate is Russia.
