Indonesia's VP offers resignation as questions mount over his eligibility
JAKARTA, Indonesia — Indonesia's vice president offered to resign during a meeting with President Prabowo Subianto on Tuesday, according to officials, adding to the turmoil at the highest levels of the country's leadership.
Vice President Gibran Rakabuming Raka, the 39-year-old son of former President Joko Widodo, held over two hours of talks with Prabowo, according to State Secretariat Minister Prasetyo Hadi.
It was not immediately clear whether Prabowo accepted the resignation, Hadi told reporters at a news conference at the presidential palace. The president advised Raka to "continue pursuing legal avenues to defend the validity of his academic documents," Hadi said.
As he left his office later in the day, Raka made a brief statement to reporters without addressing the resignation offer.
"I respect all criticism and feedback from the public regarding the developments that are taking place," Raka said. "I do not want the current situation to become a prolonged political controversy."
The resignation offer comes amid growing pressure on Raka over a court dispute involving his academic credentials. It was apparently not related to an ongoing probe into allegations that top police officials, including the president's chief of staff Gen. Listyo Sigit Prabowo, had been involved in a wiretap targeting the president. Three other police generals have also been implicated in the case.
Listyo previously served as national police chief under Widodo, who has not been implicated in the wiretapping investigation.
The developments come amid a widening political rift between Prabowo and Widodo. The popular former president backed Prabowo's presidential bid after he chose Raka as a running mate.
The controversy over Raka's academic qualifications escalated last month after the Supreme Court ruled that the documents he submitted regarding his overseas education did not meet election requirements.
The ruling intensified political pressure on Raka and fueled calls from some lawmakers for his impeachment.
Widodo faces unrelated allegations that he used a fake university diploma, which he denies.

A514.text:
US, Russia and Ukraine start second day of Abu Dhabi peace talks
ABU DHABI, Nov 11 - Russian, Ukrainian and US officials began a second day of peace talks in Abu Dhabi on Wednesday, resuming meetings which Kyiv and Washington depicted on Monday as constructive but produced no early signs of a breakthrough.
Ukrainian and Russian negotiators gave no details after Monday's talks, the first between the warring sides since February, and Moscow and Kyiv went into the talks far apart on terms for a possible settlement.
"We are starting the second day of the talks," Rustem Umerov, Ukraine's top negotiator, said on the Telegram app. "First, there will be a trilateral format with the United States and Russia. After that, we will have a separate meeting with the European partners."
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, who like Russian President Vladimir Putin is not attending the talks, said Monday's "substantive" discussions had covered humanitarian and security issues, and that a potential summit of Russian, Ukrainian and US leaders could be discussed on Tuesday.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio described the first day of talks as very productive, without giving details. The second day of talks is the last day when meetings are scheduled.
Despite public optimism from US President Donald Trump, there has been no sign of major compromises or that new issues are being discussed more than 4-1/2 years after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Russian forces control about a fifth of Ukraine, but territory is not the only issue at stake. Others include future security guarantees, which both sides want, and Moscow's demands that Ukraine adopt neutral status and not join NATO.
Each said side the other had launched attacks overnight, despite the peace talks being under way.
Russia struck six large electricity substations in Ukraine's four central regions, Ukrainian Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi said.
Drone debris killed two people after hitting an apartment building in Russia's Smolensk region bordering Belarus, the TASS news agency said, citing the regional governor.
Russia's defence ministry said its forces had struck a cargo vessel in the Black Sea southwest of the Ukrainian port city of Odesa that was carrying weapons and military equipment for Ukraine's armed forces.
Reuters could not verify the reports.
NEW ATTACKS
Trump has intensified pressure on Kyiv to reach a deal, saying it is time for Ukraine to end the war or face "a very bad thing". Last week he said the war was close to being settled in a "big beautiful agreement", but he has frequently predicted breakthroughs that have not materialised.
The new American drive for a deal has galvanized European officials into pushing for a place at the negotiating table to seek an end to Europe's deadliest conflict since World War Two.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov on Tuesday underlined Moscow's preference for negotiating a broad European security framework before tackling the specifics of the war.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said wider security talks should only come after a ceasefire. Lavrov rejected the notion of a truce, saying the Europeans were trying to secure breathing space for Ukraine.
The Kremlin said on Wednesday the Russian delegation in Abu Dhabi had not been in contact with European representatives there, and that no such contacts were planned.
In a call with reporters, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov also said that Russian President Vladimir Putin is being briefed constantly by the Russian delegation about the talks.
There has been no sign publicly that Putin is willing to drop his demand that Ukraine surrender the entire eastern region of Donbas before a peace deal can be struck.
Zelenskiy has repeatedly refused to hand over land that Ukrainian troops have died defending.

NAIROBI, Nov 11 - Kenya discharged its last Ebola patient on Wednesday, starting a 42-day countdown to when the country can be declared free of the disease, Health Minister Aden Duale said.
• Kenya has reported nine Ebola cases since early October, when a Kenyan man tested positive for the disease and died after arriving from Democratic Republic of Congo, where a large outbreak was declared in May
• The other cases were all contacts of the index case
• One of the other patients died and seven recovered
• No new infections have been recorded since October 19, the health ministry told a press conference
• The last 11 people who had come into contact with confirmed cases were released from quarantine on Wednesday, the health ministry said
• Kenya will now require citizens arriving from the Democratic Republic of Congo to undergo a 21-day quarantine, Duale said
• Ebola has been reported in four countries across eastern, central and western Africa, the widest geographic spread of any outbreak on the continent to date
• The outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo is the second-largest on record, with more than 11,000 cases confirmed REUTERS

A519.text:
Workers across Spain stage first general strike in 14 years as anger rages over housing
MADRID, Nov 11 - Spanish workers went on a general strike on Wednesday, enduring stormy weather to set up picket lines in a mass protest against the country's housing affordability crisis less than three weeks before a snap general election.
It is the first general strike in 14 years to be jointly backed by Spain's two largest unions, UGT and CCOO, as well as other labour organisations and tenants' associations angry about rising rents and evictions.
Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez hopes to harness voter resentment over housing in the November 29 election to shift the political narrative away from a series of corruption cases involving his inner circle and a deadly train crash last month. So far, his Socialist Party still trails in opinion polls.
Unions said participation in the strike was uneven across Spain, with the strongest support in coastal regions including the Cantabrian coast, Catalonia, Andalusia and parts of the Mediterranean, where housing pressures have been particularly acute.
Spain has a deficit of about 750,000 homes, which is set to grow to more than a million by 2028, according to the central bank.
With fewer people able to afford a home, renting has increased sharply, putting pressure on that market. The average rental price of €1,176 ($1,315) is equivalent to about 98.7% of a young person's average monthly salary in Spain, according to the Youth Council of Spain.
"I’m 36 years old and I still can’t move out on my own," said Madrid resident Jesus Gonzalez, 36, who works in a hospital IT department. "Rents just keep going up, house prices just keep going up, and it’s simply impossible."
EARLY TURNOUT STRONGEST AT PORTS, AUTO PLANTS
Angela de Miguel, vice president of Spain's main business lobby CEOE, said the strike was counterproductive because small businesses were also affected by the housing crisis, since shortages of homes made recruitment more challenging.
Speaking on state broadcaster TVE, she said the solution was to build more homes and to lower taxes in construction and the home-buying process, which she said had helped increase the final price of buying a new home by 40% in the past decade.
Plans for massive protest marches in the afternoon were threatened by two storms, dubbed Charles and Bruna, that led weather agency AEMET to issue alerts for 14 regions over strong winds, rough seas and heavy rains.
According to UGT and CCOO, early participation in the strike reached 90% at ports and in the automotive sector, with "total stoppages" reported at factories including Volkswagen's in Navarre and SEAT's in Barcelona.
The unions also put early turnout at 85% in the meat industry, 82% in waste collection and 75% in the energy sector. They said participation was lower in healthcare and social services, at 38%, and at 35% in the postal service.
They pointed to a 10% drop in electricity demand as an indication of disruption across energy-intensive industries, saying much of the petrochemical, steel-processing, food-processing and transport sectors had halted activity apart from operations covered by minimum service requirements.
Tensions flared at the start of the strike at Madrid's Mercamadrid wholesale market, where about 1,000 protesters gathered. CCOO's Madrid branch said on X that police fired pepper spray at pickets and arrested one of them, with 13 people requiring medical attention.
A police spokesperson confirmed the arrest but not the use of pepper spray, although he said it was used to disperse a separate picket line in the Carabanchel district.

A523.text:
PLA-linked Chinese university bought Nvidia H200 chips despite US blacklist, records show
- Northwestern Polytechnical University, on the US Entity List, bought two Nvidia H200 chips in October for 874,700 yuan, showing gaps in export controls.
- Records show Chinese defence-focused universities also rented access to restricted Nvidia chips, including H200, H100, A100 and A800 processors, through domestic suppliers.
- The findings add pressure on Nvidia and Washington, as lawmakers seek tighter chip controls while China keeps finding ways to access advanced AI computing power.
AI generated
BEIJING – A Chinese university with deep ties to the People’s Liberation Army bought Nvidia’s powerful H200 AI chips in October despite being on a US export blacklist, procurement records show, highlighting gaps in Washington’s efforts to curb China’s access to advanced technology.
The findings come as Nvidia and its CEO Jensen Huang face mounting scrutiny in Washington over his lobbying for looser restrictions on sales of AI chips to China, following reports alleging he was targeted by a Chinese spying operation.
Huang has argued that continued US sales to China would preserve American technological leadership and keep Chinese customers reliant on US technology.
But some US lawmakers say access to Nvidia’s most powerful AI chips can speed China’s development of AI systems for weapons design, intelligence analysis and military modernisation.
Both Democrats and Republicans in Congress have urged stronger controls on China’s access to advanced AI chips, such as chip-tracking requirements and greater congressional oversight of exports.
Three Republican congressional committee chairmen have requested a briefing with Huang on Nov 18 over his reported contacts with an alleged Chinese intelligence operative.
Northwestern Polytechnical University, a member of China’s Seven Sons of National Defence group of elite defence-focused universities, bought two H200 chips in October for 874,700 yuan (S$168,000), according to an Oct 21 procurement record on its website.
The chips were purchased for its management school from Shaanxi Bosuan Network Technology rather than directly from Nvidia, the record shows.
The H200 is among Nvidia’s most capable chips for training and running advanced AI systems and is subject to US export licence approvals, which are normally denied for blacklisted institutions such as Northwestern Polytechnical.
Northwestern Polytechnical also bought access to H200 chips and other powerful Nvidia AI processors in 2026 through five contracts for rented computing capacity from Chinese companies, procurement records show.
Reuters is reporting the chip purchases and computing contracts for the first time.
Northwestern Polytechnical, Nvidia and the US Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security, which oversees export controls, did not respond to requests for comment. Reuters could not determine contact details for Shaanxi Bosuan Network Technology.
Trade blacklist
Based in the northwestern city of Xian, Northwestern Polytechnical conducts research related to military aircraft, missiles and satellites.
The US Commerce Department added the university to its trade blacklist, known as the Entity List, in 2001 over its alleged involvement in missile-proliferation activities and military research.
It tightened the restrictions in 2019, making licences for exports of controlled US technology to the university subject to a policy of denial in most circumstances.
Northwestern Polytechnical’s purchases show how Chinese institutions with military ties continue to obtain US AI computing power through domestic suppliers, either by buying chips outright or renting access to servers containing them.
[truncated]

A543.text:
Rubio says ‘no need’ to attack Iran as diplomacy gathers pace
TEHRAN - Top US diplomat Marco Rubio said on Nov 10 that he saw no need to attack Iran again, as diplomatic efforts to end the war gathered steam and Tehran urged Washington to accept its demands for reopening the Strait of Hormuz.
Hours after US President Donald Trump said he saw “positive momentum” towards resolving the eight-month war, Rubio said the United States’ squeezing of Iran’s economy made further attacks unnecessary.
“The economic campaign (against Iran) is so devastating that right now there is no need for major combat operations,” the Secretary of State said after a meeting of G7 foreign ministers in Paris. “That’s what I told our allies here today.”
Iran’s efforts to blockade Hormuz, the major exit route for Gulf energy shipments, have sent oil prices soaring – a major factor in the humbling of Trump’s Republicans in last week’s midterm elections.
Washington has imposed a counter-blockade on Iranian ports and in August announced what it called an “economic asphyxiation” campaign aimed at financially strangling Iran, already battered by years of sanctions.
Britain’s Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband called for greater efforts to end the conflict, while warning of the economic damage of an ongoing impasse.
“We need to move beyond the ‘no war, no peace’ stalemate, which is causing deep economic pain for our countries,” he said in Paris.
“We must see an all-out diplomatic effort to end this conflict, prevent a nuclear Iran and the threats it poses around the world, and get the Strait of Hormuz properly reopened.”
Washington has appeared to taper down its threats of renewed strikes after the Republicans’ defeat, and even Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu – who launched the war alongside Trump and recently lobbied to “forever eliminate the existential threat of Iran” – appeared to recognise the shifting diplomatic reality.
“In the very near future, we’re going to be confronted by international pressure to accept a nuclear-armed Iran and the preservation of this terror regime that seeks to annihilate us,” he said on Nov 10.
‘Address Iran’s demands’
Tehran said its offer to reopen Hormuz within two days – if Washington agreed to a raft of conditions – remained on the table.
Iran’s demands have included ending the war on all fronts, unfreezing its assets, lifting oil sanctions and ending the US blockade of its ports.
“The conflict with Iran will not be resolved through military means, nor by intensifying sanctions,” Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told the IRNA news agency.
“The only solution is to adopt a language of respect, engage in diplomacy, and address Iran’s demands and conditions – which were outlined in the two-day proposal and remain on the table.”
Meanwhile, vessels continue to come under attack in and around the strait.
The Emirati state oil company ADNOC said on Nov 10 that one of its vessels had “sustained damage following an attack in the UAE’s territorial waters”, while the British maritime agency UKMTO reported a tanker was “struck by an unknown projectile” off the Omani coast.
Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said that three oil tankers were on fire in the Strait of Hormuz, though it was unclear whether they were referring to the same ships.
US ‘more flexible’ after midterms
On Nov 9, after meeting Qatar’s prime minister at the White House, Trump said that the US was “locked and loaded”, but further strikes were “quite unlikely” given that key US allies in the Gulf “would prefer the status quo”.
“We are seeing positive momentum toward an end to this Conflict, and will ensure that America’s interests are at all times protected,” he wrote on social media.
Qatar and Pakistan are leading diplomatic efforts to resolve the war, which began with US-Israeli strikes that killed Iran’s Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei in late February.
Qatari foreign ministry official Ibrahim al-Hashmi confirmed there had been progress in the negotiations.

NEW YORK – The US Justice Department on Nov 10 announced charges against three men it described as “Iranian operatives” over their role in an alleged terrorist plot at Britain’s RAF Fairford airbase.
Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi, Mohsen Mohajeri and Mohammad Ali al-Hassani were charged in relation to the September incident at the base, which has been used by the US military in its operations against Iran.
Police were called to the Fairford site in south-west England after a local farmer reported seeing a group of men with several white vans engaged in “suspicious” activity.
A US charging document states that Al-Hassani, 35, an Iraqi national, directed unnamed individuals to drive to the base in the vans, some of which contained barrels of fuel.
It claims that he earlier paid the group to buy metallic objects that could be used as shrapnel, and to disguise the vehicles as being engaged in fuel delivery services.
Al-Saadi, 32, a dual Iranian-Iraqi national already jailed in New York on terrorism charges, allegedly passed coded messages ahead of the plot to Al-Hassani and Mohajeri, 48, an Iranian national.
The United States abruptly withdrew all its B-1 bombers from the Royal Air Force (RAF) site following the incident.
“Anyone who plans a terrorist plot on a military base housing American service members will be prosecuted by the United States government,” said Attorney-General Todd Blanche.
The trio were charged in an eight-count indictment that alleges their involvement in several other plots in support of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and pro-Iranian group Kataeb Hezbollah. AFP

Brigadier-General Sean Stinchon, the commanding general of US Army Counterintelligence Command, added: “The alleged conduct of a senior soldier, entrusted with sensitive information, is a sobering reminder that insider threats are real and persistent.”

A561.text:
Carney says he will tell Xi that outsiders should not meddle in Canada’s affairs
OTTAWA, Nov 10 - Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Tuesday he would stress to Chinese President Xi Jinping later this month that China and other countries should not interfere in Canada's internal affairs.
Carney said he would meet Xi on the sidelines of an APEC summit in Shenzhen on November 18-19.
In April 2025, Carney said China was one of the largest threats with respect to foreign interference. In 2024, a probe into meddling from abroad heard that Canada's spy agency concluded China had interfered in the 2019 and 2021 elections.
"The advantage of these meetings is you can raise issues directly and frankly. And I will be raising the importance with which we attach to the non-interference in our affairs by China and other countries," Carney told reporters.
Beijing has long denied it seeks to interfere in Canadian domestic affairs.
As part of a bid to reduce economic dependence on the United States, Canada is seeking tighter ties with China after a long spell of chilly bilateral relations.
In February, after a visit by Carney, China said it would suspend some tariffs on Canadian agricultural products imposed during a trade dispute. REUTERS

A58.text:
Three Iran-backed suspects plotted attacks including RAF Fairford incident, US says
- Published
The US Department of Justice (DOJ) has announced charges against three Iran-backed operatives that it alleges were involved in a string of plots in the US and Europe.
The DOJ said Iranian agents most recently "orchestrated a terrorist plot at an air force base in the United Kingdom", saying they were involved in the major incident in September near RAF Fairford in the UK, where US armed forces were stationed.
One man, a dual Iranian-Iraqi national, is accused of communicating with contacts in the UK from a prison in New York where he is awaiting trial on previous charges. The other two are accused of doing the same from Iran.
Iran has strongly denied any involvement in the RAF Fairford incident.
Seven men have been arrested in the UK over the incident, which came to light when suspicious vans were reported near the RAF base.
Iranian Mohsen Mohajeri, Iraqi national Mohammad Ali al-Hassani and dual Iranian-Iraqi citizen Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi were charged in an indictment unsealed on Tuesday, the DOJ said.
It accuses the trio of planning attacks in Europe that were carried out under the name of a purportedly new group with the pseudonym Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya (The Islamic Movement of the People of the Right Hand - HAYI).
"Of the 18 terrorist attacks in the spring of 2026 for which HAYI claimed responsibility in Europe, seven took place in the UK," the DOJ statement said. It added that the attacks involved "arsons, explosives, and in one instance, a near-fatal stabbing in London of two Jewish men, including a dual US-British citizen".
Two Jewish men were stabbed in Golders Green, north London, in April. A suspect is due to stand trial next year.
"This eight-count indictment shows the determination of Iran to commit terrorist attacks in Europe and the US," FBI Director Kash Patel said.
He added that one of the three "allegedly sent coded messages to assist in future acts of violence" from detention.
Patel said the accused were involved in nearly 20 attempted attacks in support of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and the Iran-backed Iraqi militia Kataib Hezbollah.
A major incident was declared on 27 September near the UK's RAF Fairford base, in the Cotswolds in Gloucestershire, after three suspicious vans were seen near the airbase.
No explosive materials were found in the vans, but a quantity of petrol was seized.
The DOJ said that in August, al-Hassani "allegedly directed and paid associates" in the UK to "conduct preparatory steps and arrange logistics for the RAF Fairford terrorist plot".
On 22 August, al-Hassani paid one individual to "perform pre-operational surveillance of RAF Fairford's perimeter", the department said.
In September, al-Hassani paid several people to help him prepare for the plot, the DOJ also alleged.
According to its statement, this included "procuring vans and barrels of fuel, researching the purchase of chemical accelerants, including large quantities of potassium chloride, and purchasing metallic objects that could be used as explosive shrapnel".
The suspects then gave the vans an appearance of being used by a fuel delivery business and a swimming pool supply business, the DOJ stated.
"On 26 September, al-Hassani allegedly tasked individuals to drive three vans, some of which were later determined to contain barrels of fuel, to the RAF Fairford base."
The DOJ also said al-Hassani was "in frequent communication" with the van drivers and helped to direct them where to drive.
"At least two of the three vans, while en route to the perimeter of RAF Fairford, encountered a security roadblock and were not allowed to proceed on their intended route," it added.
It was in the very early hours of 27 September, that the vans were spotted by a local farmer who was heading home from a party, and called the police.

A589.text:
Morning opening: Zelenskyy ‘happy’ with US envoys’ approach during Russia talks as day two to begin
Jakub Krupa
Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he was “happy” with US mediators’ “changes” in approach during the first day of the trilateral talks with Russia on ending the invasion of Ukraine.
Speaking in Copenhagen last night, Zelenskyy praised the talks as “constructive and quite substantive,” hoping for more progress to be made today.
But he also hit out at Russia’s assessment of its battlefield strengths, saying Vladimir Putin lives in a “different reality”. In a post on social media, Zelenskyy said Russia has claimed at the talks that they occupied half of the Donbas in Ukraine’s east.
“This is the problem. Putin lives in a different reality,” the Ukrainian president wrote, adding: “I can draw a picture for him too where I fully occupy Russia. But it’s not true. What was good is that the American side confirmed the Ukrainian assessment of what is happening on the battlefield.”
We will hear from him later as he is expected to address the Danish parliament late morning.
US envoys Jared Kushner and businessman Steve Witkoff are mediating the negotiations. Kushner told delegates the US had “narrowed the gaps” between the warring sides, without providing details, and hoped to move towards a “solution” to Europe’s worst conflict since the second world war.
Elsewhere, I will bring you the latest from Bulgaria as it marks a national day of mourning after a deadly motorway accident which killed 11 and left over 50 injured, from Latvia and Lithuania after a tricky night with several air threat alerts in both countries, from Portugal as the country braces for the impact of storm Charles, from Spain where a general strike gets under way, and from Poland with its independence day celebrations.
Lots for us to cover today.
It’s Wednesday, 11 November 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.
Reuters is reporting via sources that the trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi have now concluded.
No point in speculating on what it could mean: they might have agreed on something last night and had to OK it with the ultimate bosses overnight, or…?
Let’s see. We will no doubt hear from them at some point today.
There are few illussions that an immediate breakthrough is possible - snap analysis
Pjotr Sauer
The second and final day of US-brokered peace talks between Russia and Ukraine is underway in Abu Dhabi, with Moscow and Kyiv holding their first direct negotiations in nine months.
Both sides have sent high-level delegations, although neither Vladimir Putin nor Volodymyr Zelenskyy is attending.
Ukraine and the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, described the first day of talks as “constructive”, though there are few illusions that an immediate breakthrough is on the horizon.
The biggest obstacle remains Russia’s far-reaching demands, particularly its insistence that Ukraine withdraw from the entire Donbas region, including areas still under Kyiv’s control.
There are also growing fears in Europe that Washington and Moscow could reach a broader agreement that would see Nato scale back its military presence in eastern Europe, potentially leaving allies more vulnerable to Russian pressure at a time of historic tensions with the west.
In an effort to shape the direction of the talks, European leaders have sent several envoys to Abu Dhabi, though they are not believed to be directly involved in the negotiations.
Russia arrests two 'agents' of Polish intelligence in Kaliningrad
Separately, Russian security services (FSB) said that two “agents” working for Polish intelligence had been arrested in the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, which borders Poland and Lithuania, AFP reported.
The pair were allegedly part of Poland’s internal security agency and were collecting information on the “servicemen and facilities of the Russian Ministry of Defence”, according to the FSB, which did not disclose their identities or nationalities.

A592.text:
A Kenyan mother in Saudi Arabia has reportedly been sentenced to 100 lashes after giving birth outside marriage.
Under the Saudi sharia law system, sex outside marriage is a criminal offence. But it is women who are disproportionately targeted, say rights groups, which have condemned the punishment as an “act of violence”.
Although many unmarried women give birth in Saudi Arabia, rights groups say the Kenyan mother’s case only came to light because she had been taken to a hospital, which are required to report single women giving birth to the authorities.
“Most of them give birth at home, that’s why they aren’t reported,” said Ekaterina Porras Sivolobova, founder of Do Bold, a non-profit organisation advocating for migrant workers’ rights in the Gulf.
The Kenyan mother, Esther Wanja Muthoni, was a domestic worker recruited to work as housekeeper and nanny in Saudi Arabia. She reportedly became pregnant during a brief relationship with an Egyptian man and said that the child’s father had since left the country.
A 2024 Guardian investigation found a number of Kenyan single mothers were abandoned by their children’s fathers out of fear of being arrested for having extramarital sex. After the ruling, which was issued last month, Muthoni told the New York Times she was afraid about not being able to endure the lashes and said: “I don’t deserve this.”
The case comes as a planned visit to Saudi Arabia by Reem Alsalem, the UN special rapporteur on violence against women and girls, was postponed last week. Alsalem said she had intended to “raise the situation of specific cases during the visit. If the visit does not take place soon, I will do so separately through the established channels that we have as mandate holders.”
Maryam Aldossari, acting director at the UK-based rights organisation ALQST (al-qist means “justice” in Arabic), said the ruling was an act of violence and the woman should have been sent back to Kenya and not punished.
“It just shows the hypocrisy behind so-called Saudi reform. We know MBS [Mohammed bin Salman, the Saudi crown prince] has been trying to show the world that Saudi is becoming a modern country that empowers women, yet we see the court sentence a mother to 100 lashes,” said Aldossari.
In April 2020, Saudi announced a reform to end flogging as a judicial punishment. However, it only applied to ta’zir offences, where judges have discretion over punishments. Although most flogging sentences fell into this category, flogging remained a possible punishment for certain hudud (fixed punishments under Islamic law) offences, such as alcohol consumption and adultery, ALQST said in a report in 2021.
Sivolobova said it had been difficult to help in cases involving Kenyan mothers compared with those from other countries. “I haven’t been able to get help from the Kenyan authorities to support these women,” she said.
The Saudi government was approached for comment.

A597.text:
'The dinosaurs did not have a lobby. Fossil fuels do.' - UN chief
Oliver Milman
Guterres launches into a plea for accelerated action to cut emissions and takes direct aim at the fossil fuel industry. The UN chief has already called on countries to push forward a phase out of fossil fuels, rather than merely hinting at it, here at Cop.
“The case for fossil fuels is collapsing,” he said. “Fossil fuels must go the way of the dinosaurs. And that won’t happen on its own. The dinosaurs did not have a lobby. Fossil fuels do.”
“It’s time to kick the habit – and end the fossil-fuel addiction,” he said. Guterres likes a good pun and one of his final climate speeches has a decent one: “It’s make or bake time.”
Next up is Abiy Ahmed, prime minister of Ethiopia, which is hosting next year’s Cop. Ahmed lauds the country’s effort to plant millions of trees, which is “teaching us to live in harmony with nature and care about what we leave for our children.”
Ethiopia is doing its bit by banning the import of petrol and diesel cars and deploying renewable energy but requires more help with access to finance, the prime minister added. High borrowing costs is hindering developing countries from building resilience to the climate crisis, Ahmed said, adding that “lowering them is a test of collective credibiliy.”
Albanese says Australia is “playing its part” and points to the country’s substantial record on renewable energy that he says is now half the country’s electricity. Renewable energy has doubled in just six years.
“We must share the opportunities that climate action creates, with the people who need them most.”
He pleaded with the conference to listen to existential concerns of the Pacific, and said he was approaching this issue in the same way he had approached his political life, with “no one left behind.”
Then he’s done. And he didn’t mention the phrase “fossil fuels”.
And after the UN secretary general told the Cop31 that developed countries had to get off fossil fuels, we now have the Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese. The PM of one of the world’s biggest fossil fuel exporters.
Guterres finishes up by thanking young people, activists, scientists, Indigenous people and others for their advocacy before noting that he will be standing down as UN chief at the end of the year.
Despite this “I will not stop telling the truth and I will not stop fighting for it,” he said, to applause and a single loud whoop.
“I will be standing side-by-side with you as an advocate and an ally,” he said. “Together, let’s keep telling the truth about the climate crisis. Let’s keep demanding the action that truth requires. And let’s keep fighting for the sustainable future we know is in our hands. I will be with you every step of the way.”
And with that Guterres shuffles off stage, his last Cop speech finished.
It may not be as dazzling as a man with glittering trousers and a billowing shirt whirling around on stage in front of shots of mountains, but Guterres is starkly laying out the challenge faced by countries.
Coal must be gone in about 15 years, oil and gas use slashed by a third, he reminds everyone.
“We have a choice: Either plan this just transition – or pay for it in chaos and lost livelihoods,” he says.
Guterres then notes the huge profits of fossil fuel companies and compares it to the relatively small amount of money given to the loss and damage fund for vulnerable countries. This inequity should be remedied by a windfall tax on oil and gas companies he said, to applause.
“It’s time for governments to tax these windfall profits – and use them to help vulnerable countries recover,” he said. “Polluters must pay.”

A81.text:
World
3 charged in U.S. with planning terror attacks, including alleged planned assault on British airbase
1 suspect allegedly continued to co-ordinate U.K. attack after arrest months earlier, U.S. attorney says
Three men, including one already jailed in the United States, were accused by U.S. authorities Tuesday of being Iran-supported operatives who plotted nearly 20 attacks on Jewish communities in Europe and the U.S. as well as a planned assault on a British airbase used by the U.S. Air Force.
Charges against Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi, a dual Iranian-Iraqi national; Mohsen Mohajeri, an Iranian national; and Mohammad Ali al-Hassani, an Iraqi national, were outlined in a superseding indictment unsealed in Manhattan federal court. Only al-Saadi is in custody.
U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald in New York said in a news release that al-Saadi, who was arrested in the spring, allegedly continued to co-ordinate with his co-defendants in the days leading up to the attempted September terrorist plot at a British Royal Air Force Base in Fairford, United Kingdom, where U.S. bombers and troops had been stationed.
"These defendants helped orchestrate a campaign of terror on behalf of terrorist organizations affiliated with Iran that targeted Jewish communities in Europe and the United States, and the British military base, RAF Fairford, housing American service members," McDonald said. "The threat presented by Iran and Iran-backed terrorist groups to America and our allies is not hypothetical — it is very real."
Attorney General Todd Blanche said: "Anyone who plans a terrorist plot on a military base housing American servicemembers will be prosecuted by the United States government."
The new indictment offers fresh insight into an episode that has been shrouded in mystery for more than a month after five men were detained after midnight on Sept. 27 on suspected explosives and terrorism offenses after three suspicious vans were spotted travelling toward the base in western England.
A sixth suspect, a British-Iranian dual national, was arrested several days later. All the men were released on bail.
- U.K. charges 2 men, accuses them of working on Iran's behalf in incident at airbase
- Canada, U.K. allies vow action after RAF Fairford terror plot
British authorities linked the incident to Tehran, and though Iran denied involvement, the arrests prompted the U.S. to withdraw its bombers that had been stationed there. The bombers were redeployed to their home bases in the United States.
RAF Fairford, located 160 kilometres west of London, has been used by American bombers during decades of conflicts in the Middle East.
According to the indictment, al-Saadi allegedly used coded language in communications with relatives from jail to direct that money be passed along to others who could carry out attacks.
The indictment alleged that the three men conspired together to use a network of contacts in the United Kingdom to commit terrorist attacks on behalf of an Iran-aligned terrorist network, which included the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and Kata’ib Hezbollah.
In June, al-Saadi pleaded not guilty to charges that he plotted at least 18 attacks in Europe in retaliation for the U.S. and Israel’s war with Iran. He called himself a "prisoner of war." He has been held without bail since. His lawyers did not immediately respond to requests for comment Tuesday on the latest development.
Both Kata’ib Hezbollah and Iran’s IRGC have been designated by the U.S. government as foreign terrorist organizations. U.S. prosecutors say Al-Saadi was a Kata’ib Hezbollah commander.
